analysis.one_liner: Lets Black farmers whose USDA discrimination claims were rejected as late sue for a merits decision.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a House vote; it sat in the Judiciary Committee until the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: In 1999, the federal government settled a class action, Pigford v. Glickman, with Black farmers who said the Department of Agriculture discriminated against them in farm lending. Farmers who missed the settlement's filing deadline could only ask permission to join late; many late filers never got any decision on whether they were actually discriminated against. This bill would let any of them file a civil lawsuit to get a full decision on the merits, and it directs that the law be read broadly to serve that purpose.
analysis.who_benefits: Black farmers who filed late under the 1999 Pigford consent decree and were never given a determination on the merits of their discrimination claims. The bill would give them a route to federal court and directs courts to construe it liberally so each denied claim gets a full hearing.

how_it_helps.text: Any Pigford claimant who has never obtained a determination on the merits of a claim may obtain one through a civil action.
The bill states it is Congress' intent that the provision be liberally construed to effectuate its remedial purpose of giving a full merits determination to each denied Pigford claim.

analysis.who_pays: The Department of Agriculture and, ultimately, taxpayers, if farmers win judgments in the new civil suits. The government would also bear the cost of defending the litigation.

drawbacks.text: The bill reopens litigation over claims resolved under the 1999 consent decree, creating new lawsuits against USDA and potential federal payouts, with the government covering the cost of defending them.

The bill only opens the courthouse door; a late-filing claimant would still have to prove a discrimination complaint as defined and documented under the consent decree, so many could bring suits and still lose after years of litigation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a genuine second chance at a hearing for a group that the 1999 settlement's deadline left in limbo; the cost is new litigation and possible judgments for USDA. The bill is narrowly drawn — it covers only people who already submitted late-filing requests — so the exposure is bounded, but the litigation burden on both sides is real.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 9, 2006, with six original sponsors and cosponsors listed, including Republicans Chabot and Sensenbrenner and Democrats Scott of Virginia, Jackson-Lee, Watt, and Thompson of Mississippi.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary, its only committee assignment.
No further action was ever taken on the bill, and it received no vote before the 109th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: USDA and the federal treasury are better off, because no new discrimination suits or potential payouts were opened. The late-filing farmers got nothing this session.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: USDA avoided suits; farmers got nothing

for.name: Rep. F. James Sensenbrenner
for.role: Original cosponsor; chaired the House Judiciary Committee to which the bill was referred

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it was never reported out or scheduled for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Republican and the 10 cosponsors split 8 Democrats and 2 Republicans, so no party bloc lined up against the bill's substance; it simply received no committee action.

industries.note: The bill would expose USDA to new civil suits and possible judgments on discrimination claims it had not decided on the merits. The government's interest in avoiding those payouts ran against the farmers seeking a hearing.
